title: Structural Engineer Enquiry Form: What to Ask Before You Quote
metaTitle: Structural Engineer Enquiry Form | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: What to put on a structural engineer enquiry form so you can price jobs faster: the fields to ask, what to leave out, and UK and Australian privacy basics.
geoDirectAnswer: A structural engineer enquiry form should ask for contact details, the client's role, site location, job type, project stage, drawings or photos, and timing, with optional notes. Leave out data you don't need to quote, add a short privacy note with a link to your policy, and tell people when you'll reply.
keyTakeaways: A structured fee proposal form gets you the details to price a job without rounds of emails.
Ask for role, site location, job type, project stage, files and timing; keep free text optional.
The ICO's data minimisation principle says collect only what you need, not data that might be useful later.
UK and Australian privacy guidance both point to telling people at the point of collection why you need their details.
Use the form's answers to route enquiries automatically and set clear expectations about your reply.
contentMarkdown:
Most structural engineering websites end with the same form: name, email, phone, message. Then the back-and-forth starts. Where is the property? What kind of job is it? Are there drawings? Has the builder been appointed? By the time you have enough to price the work, the client may have accepted a quote from someone who asked the right questions first. A well-designed structural engineer enquiry form fixes that. It collects what you need to prepare a fee proposal in one go, filters out jobs you don't do, and shows the client you know what you're doing. This guide covers what to ask, what not to ask, and the privacy basics for firms in Australia and the UK.

### Why the standard contact form costs you work

A blank "message" box puts the work on the client, and many clients don't know what an engineer needs. You get "Need an engineer for an extension, please call", and the job starts with a phone call or three emails before you can even estimate the fee.

A structured fee proposal request form changes that. The client answers a few specific questions, attaches what they have, and you can reply with a fee or a short list of follow-up questions. It also helps you sort enquiries: a homeowner wanting a wall removed and a developer with a multi-storey project need very different responses.

### What to ask on a structural engineer enquiry form

Keep it short enough to finish on a phone, and ask only what changes your fee or your decision to quote.

#### 1. Who the client is

- Name, email and phone
- Their role: homeowner, builder, architect or designer, developer, strata or body corporate, other

The role tells you how they'll brief you and who else is involved. An architect will usually send drawings; a homeowner may need guidance on what to provide.

#### 2. Where the site is

- Site address or suburb/town and postcode

Location affects travel time, local council or building control requirements, and whether the job is in your service area at all. If you only cover certain areas, say so next to this field.

#### 3. What the job is

A dropdown or checkboxes work better than free text here. Typical options:

- Wall removal or opening
- Extension or alteration
- New build
- Inspection or structural report (for example cracking, movement, pre-purchase)
- Retaining wall
- Remedial or repair design
- Certification or sign-off
- Civil: drainage, subdivision, driveways or similar
- Other (with a short description)

#### 4. What stage the project is at

- Just exploring
- Architectural drawings in progress
- Drawings complete, ready for engineering
- Builder appointed or works started
- Works complete, need inspection or certification

Stage tells you urgency and scope. A job where works have started and the builder is waiting is very different from early design.

#### 5. Files

- Upload drawings, plans or photos (PDF, JPG, PNG, DWG if you accept it)

For inspections, photos of cracks or defects are often very useful. Set a sensible file size limit and say what it is.

#### 6. Timing

- When do you need the engineering by?

#### 7. A short description

- Anything else we should know?

Put this last and keep it optional. By now the structured answers have covered the essentials.

### What not to ask

Extra fields can put people off finishing the form, and collecting data you don't need creates privacy obligations.

The UK's data minimisation principle is a useful test even if you're in Australia. The ICO's guidance on [data minimisation](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) says personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for your purpose. It adds that you must not collect personal data on the off-chance that it might be useful in the future.

For an enquiry form, that usually means leaving out:

- date of birth
- full postal address of the client when you only need the site address
- budget, unless it genuinely affects whether you'll quote
- marketing preferences bundled into a required field

### Privacy notices: UK and Australia

#### UK

The ICO's guidance on the [right to be informed](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-be-informed/) says you must give people privacy information at the time you collect their data. That includes your purposes, lawful basis, retention period and who you share the data with, in clear and plain language. A short note under the form with a link to your full privacy notice is a practical way to do this.

#### Australia

The OAIC's guidelines on [APP 5](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-5-app-5-notification-of-the-collection-of-personal-information) explain that an APP entity collecting personal information must take reasonable steps to notify the person of certain matters, or ensure they're aware of them. These include its identity and contact details, the purposes of collection, its usual disclosures and information about its privacy policy. These steps should be taken at or before the time of collection where practicable.

For online forms, the OAIC's examples of reasonable steps include clearly and prominently displaying these matters in the form, or providing a readily accessible and prominent link to a notice. Whether the Privacy Act applies to your firm depends on your circumstances, so check the OAIC's current guidance. This isn't legal advice.

Either way, the practical step is the same: a brief, plain-English note under the form explaining why you're collecting the details and what you'll do with them, plus a link to your privacy policy.

### Example: before and after

Here's an invented example of the same enquiry coming through two different forms.

**Before (basic contact form):** "Hi, need an engineer for my house. Can you call me? – Sam"

**After (structured form):**

| Field | Answer |
|---|---|
| Role | Homeowner |
| Site | Suburb and postcode within your service area |
| Job type | Wall removal or opening |
| Stage | Architectural drawings complete |
| Files | Floor plan PDF, two photos of the wall |
| Timing | Builder starting in six weeks |
| Notes | Load-bearing wall between kitchen and dining room |

With the second version you can check the drawings and estimate the fee straight away, often without needing a call first.

### Making the form work harder

#### Route enquiries automatically

Use the job type and stage answers to send each enquiry to the right engineer, tag it in your CRM and trigger the right reply. An inspection request might get an automatic email asking for more photos, while a new build goes straight to a senior engineer. My guide to [automating lead triage into your CRM](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html) shows how.

#### Set expectations after submitting

The confirmation message and email should say what happens next and roughly when you'll reply, for example "We'll review your drawings and send a fee proposal or questions within two working days". Then stick to it.

#### Put the form where people decide

Link to it from every service page and service-area page, not just the contact page. If you're working on local visibility, my guide to [local SEO for structural engineers](/blog/local-seo-for-structural-engineers.html) covers those pages.

### Enquiry form checklist

| Field or feature | Include? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Name, email, phone | Yes | To reply |
| Client role | Yes | Shapes your response |
| Site location | Yes | Travel, local rules, service area |
| Job type (dropdown) | Yes | Fee and who handles it |
| Project stage | Yes | Urgency and scope |
| File upload | Yes | Drawings and photos speed up pricing |
| Timing | Yes | Prioritising work |
| Free-text notes | Optional | Anything the fields missed |
| Date of birth, budget | Usually no | Not needed to quote |
| Privacy note and link | Yes | UK and Australian privacy guidance |
| Clear confirmation message | Yes | Sets expectations |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for structural and civil engineering consultancies in Australia and the UK, including fee proposal forms with file uploads, routing to the right engineer, and privacy notes set up properly. You can see more about my [websites for structural engineers](/industries/structural-engineers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like fewer back-and-forth emails before you can quote, [get in touch](/#contact) and I'll tell you what I'd change on your current form.

title: Fractional CFO Case Studies: How to Write Them for Your Website
metaTitle: Fractional CFO Case Studies | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to write fractional CFO case studies that win discovery calls: a simple structure, client confidentiality, and FTC rules on testimonials and results.
geoDirectAnswer: A strong fractional CFO case study describes the client by industry and stage, states the problem in plain language, explains the specific work and time frame, and reports outcomes you can back up. Get written permission for names and quotes, label illustrative examples clearly, disclose unexpected connections and don't imply one client's results are typical.
keyTakeaways: Specific case studies differentiate a fractional CFO website far more than generic service taglines.
Use the same five parts every time: client, problem, what you did, what changed and an approved quote.
Anonymized case studies are fine; presenting a made-up story as a real client is not.
The FTC says endorsements must be honest, and results must not be implied as typical without support.
Testimonials on your own website are your responsibility under the FTC's reviews and testimonials rule.
contentMarkdown:
Most fractional CFO websites say the same things: "strategic financial leadership", "scale with confidence", "CFO-level insight without the full-time cost". Founders read a dozen of these before they book a call, and the sites blur together. Fractional CFO case studies are what separate you. A specific story about a business like theirs, with a clear problem, what you did and what changed, does more than any tagline. This guide covers how to write case studies for your fractional CFO website, how to handle client confidentiality, and the US rules on testimonials and results claims you need to respect.

### Why case studies matter more than taglines

A founder hiring a fractional CFO is trusting you with their numbers, their board and often their fundraising. They want evidence that you've dealt with situations like theirs. Generic service pages can't give them that; a good case study can.

Case studies also help you get found. A page about "preparing a SaaS business for its Series A" or "fixing cash flow at a growing manufacturer" matches the specific problems owners search for, and gives AI search tools concrete material to cite. My guide to [GEO and AEO](/blog/geo-aeo-generative-engine-optimization-guide.html) explains why specific, well-structured pages perform better there.

### A simple structure that works

Keep every case study to the same five parts so readers can scan them quickly.

#### 1. The client, described the way they'd describe themselves

Industry, size or stage, and location if relevant: "a 40-person B2B software company preparing to raise", "a family-owned distributor with two warehouses". If you can't name the client, this line does the work of making the story recognizable.

#### 2. The problem in their words

What was keeping the founder up at night? Month-end close taking weeks, no reliable cash forecast, a board asking questions nobody could answer, an investor data room that didn't exist. Use the language a founder would use, not finance jargon.

#### 3. What you did

The specific work: built a 13-week cash flow forecast, rebuilt the chart of accounts, introduced monthly board packs, prepared the financial model and data room, renegotiated payment terms. Mention the time frame and how many days a month you worked with them. This shows prospects what an engagement with you actually looks like.

#### 4. What changed

Outcomes, described accurately. Faster month-end close, a forecast the board trusts, a completed raise, an exit process that ran to timetable. If you use numbers, use real ones from the engagement and be ready to back them up. See the rules below before you publish any figures.

#### 5. A quote, if the client agrees

A short, honest quote from the founder adds a human voice. Get written permission for the wording and for how they're identified.

### Confidentiality: named, anonymized or composite?

Finance work is sensitive, so many clients won't want to be named. You have three honest options:

| Approach | What it looks like | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| Named | Company name, founder name and quote, with written permission | Clients happy to be public, often after an exit or raise |
| Anonymized | "A Series A SaaS company in Austin", details changed only where they'd identify the client | Most engagements |
| Clearly labeled example | "Here's how an engagement typically runs", not presented as a real client | When you have no permissioned stories yet |

What you must not do is present a made-up story as a real client engagement. If an example is illustrative, say so.

### The US rules on testimonials and results

The FTC's rules on endorsements and reviews apply to how you present client stories and quotes on your own website.

#### Endorsements must be honest and typical results matter

The FTC's [Endorsement Guides Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking) says endorsements must be honest and not misleading, and must reflect the honest opinion of the endorser. An endorsement can't be used to make a claim the marketer couldn't legally make directly.

The same guidance explains that if an advertiser doesn't have proof that an endorser's experience represents what people will generally achieve, an ad featuring that endorser must make clear what the generally expected results are. For a fractional CFO, that means a headline result from one standout client shouldn't be presented as what every client can expect. Add context, such as the starting point and the work involved, and avoid implying it's typical unless you can support that.

#### Disclose connections readers wouldn't expect

The Endorsement Guides Q&A also says that if there's a connection between an endorser and the business that readers wouldn't expect, and it would affect how they view the endorsement, it should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. Its examples include an endorser who is a relative or employee, or who has been paid or given something of value. If a "client testimonial" comes from a friend, a referral partner or someone who received a discount for it, say so.

#### Testimonials on your site are your responsibility

The FTC's [Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers) says a business that puts testimonials on its own website is disseminating them, not merely hosting them, and could be liable if they're fake or false.

The FTC notes that its staff guidance isn't definitive and depends on the facts. Check the current guidance and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### Before and after: a case study summary

Here's an invented example of the same engagement written two ways.

**Before:** "We partnered with an exciting tech company to transform their finance function and unlock growth. The results were amazing!"

**After:** "**Client:** a 35-person B2B software company preparing for its first institutional raise. **Problem:** management accounts took six weeks, and there was no forecast investors could rely on. **What we did:** two days a month for nine months; rebuilt the month-end process, introduced a rolling 13-week cash forecast and a three-statement model, and prepared the data room. **What changed:** month-end now closes within the second week, and the founder used the model and data room throughout the raise. **Note:** results depend on each business's starting point."

The second version is specific, verifiable and honest about context. It's also more persuasive.

### Where case studies should live on your site

- **A case studies index**, filterable by industry and service, linked from your main navigation.
- **One page per case study**, so each can rank for its own problem and be shared on its own.
- **Short excerpts on service pages.** Put the cash-flow case study on your cash-flow forecasting page, and the fundraising story on your fundraising support page.
- **A strong call to action at the end**: "Facing something similar? Book a 30-minute call."

For the rest of the site, my guide to [what a fractional CFO website should include](/blog/fractional-cfo-website.html) covers service pages, pricing models and contact forms.

### Case study checklist

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Client described by industry, size and stage | Recognizable to similar founders |
| Problem in plain language | Matches what prospects search for |
| Specific work, time frame and days per month | Shows what an engagement looks like |
| Outcomes you can back up | Accurate, with context |
| Written permission for names and quotes | Protects the client relationship |
| Illustrative examples clearly labeled | Never presented as real clients |
| Unexpected connections disclosed | FTC Endorsement Guides |
| No implied "typical" results without support | FTC Endorsement Guides |
| Own page plus excerpts on service pages | Better for search and sales |

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for fractional CFO and outsourced finance firms in the US, the UK and Australia, including the Longfield Financial Advisory website in the UK. That includes case study libraries filterable by industry and service, clear service pages and booking forms. You can see more about my [websites for fractional CFO firms](/industries/fractional-cfo/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like help turning past engagements into case studies that win calls, [get in touch](/#contact).

Give context such as the starting point and the work involved, and don't imply one client's results are what everyone can expect. The FTC says an ad must make clear the generally expected results if an endorser's experience isn't typical.

title: Business Broker Valuation Page: Turn "What's It Worth?" Into Listings
metaTitle: Business Broker Valuation Page | Hamid Ali Asad
metaDescription: How to build a business broker valuation page that brings in sellers: what to explain, calculators done safely, the form to use and US and UK ad rules.
geoDirectAnswer: A business broker valuation page should explain in plain English how businesses are valued, what drives value up and down, and exactly what the owner gets when they ask. Use a short, confidential form with revenue and profit bands, label any calculator as an indicative range, and make only claims you can back up.
keyTakeaways: A valuation page answers the question owners ask first and starts a relationship before they choose a broker.
Explain how value is worked out and what you offer, rather than promising a precise number online.
If you use a calculator, show a labeled range, explain its limits and route the owner to a person.
The FTC requires a reasonable basis for ad claims, and the CAP Code requires evidence for objective claims before publishing.
In the UK, only call a valuation free if the owner pays nothing beyond the unavoidable cost of responding.
contentMarkdown:
"What's my business worth?" is often the first question an owner has when they start thinking about selling. It may be months or years before they're ready to list. A business broker valuation page answers that question in a way that starts a relationship with you, rather than sending the owner to a free online calculator that spits out a number and forgets them. This guide covers what to put on a valuation page, whether to use a calculator, what to ask on the form, and the US and UK advertising rules that apply to claims about value.

### Why a valuation page is a seller lead source

Most owners aren't ready to talk about listing the first time they visit your site. They are, however, curious about value. A page built around that question:

- matches what they're already searching for
- gives you a reason to talk before they've chosen a broker
- lets you start a conversation months before a listing, when you can help them prepare

The goal isn't to give a precise number online. It's to explain how value is worked out, set realistic expectations and make it easy to ask you for a proper, confidential opinion.

### What to put on a business broker valuation page

#### Explain how businesses are valued, in plain English

Owners often have a number in their head that's based on revenue, a friend's sale or a headline. Explain the basics of how your firm approaches value: earnings and cash flow, how adjustments for owner's pay and one-off costs work, why recurring revenue and customer concentration matter, and how the market for that kind of business affects the price. You don't need formulas; you need to show you know what you're doing and that value depends on detail.

#### Say what drives value up and down

A short list helps owners see what to work on: clean financial records, a business that runs without the owner, diversified customers, documented processes, contracts that transfer. This makes the page useful even for owners who aren't selling yet, and it naturally leads to "talk to us about preparing your business".

#### Be clear about what you offer

Spell out what the owner gets when they ask:

- an indicative range after a short call
- a written opinion of value
- a formal valuation, and whether that's a separate paid service

Say whether there's a fee and what's included. Vague offers create suspicion.

#### Show relevant experience

Sectors and deal sizes you work with, and anonymized examples of businesses you've sold, used with permission. If you show a closed deal, describe it accurately.

#### Make the next step confidential and easy

A short form or a booking link, with a clear statement about confidentiality and who will see the information.

### Should you use an online valuation calculator?

Calculators can attract visitors and capture contact details, but they come with risks. An automated number can anchor an owner on an unrealistic figure before you've seen the books. And if the tool presents its output as more reliable than it is, you may have an advertising problem (see below).

If you use one:

- **Show a range, not a single figure.**
- **Label it clearly** as an indicative estimate based only on the figures entered, not a valuation.
- **Explain the main limitations** next to the result: it doesn't account for the quality of earnings, customer concentration, industry conditions or deal terms.
- **Route to a human.** The result should lead straight to "book a confidential call to discuss your business".

A simpler, lower-risk alternative is a short form that asks for a few figures and promises a personal response within a set time.

### What to ask on the valuation request form

Keep it short and ask only what you need for a first conversation.

| Field | Why it helps |
|---|---|
| Name, email, phone | To reply |
| Type of business and location | Sector and market matter to value |
| Approximate annual revenue (band) | Sizes the opportunity |
| Approximate profit or owner's earnings (band) | The starting point for most valuations |
| Years trading | Track record |
| Reason for asking (selling soon, planning, curious) | Sets the tone of your reply |
| Preferred contact method and time | Respects privacy and schedules |

Use bands rather than exact figures in the first step. Owners may be more comfortable sharing ranges before they know you, and you'll get the detail later.

#### Don't over-collect

The UK ICO's guidance on [data minimisation](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) says personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for your purpose, and that you must not collect personal data on the off-chance it might be useful in the future. Even if you work only in the US, it's a sensible standard for a form that asks owners about their finances. Link to your privacy policy next to the form.

### Advertising rules: what you can claim about value

Valuation pages often make claims: "free valuation", "we get owners the best price", "our clients sell for more". These are advertising claims, and both the US and UK have rules about them.

#### United States

The FTC's [Advertising FAQs for small business](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/advertising-faqs-guide-small-business) set out the basic principles under the FTC Act: advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive, advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims, and ads cannot be unfair. The FAQ explains that before an ad runs, a company has to have a "reasonable basis" for its claims, meaning objective evidence. It also notes that statements from satisfied customers usually aren't enough to support a claim that requires objective evaluation.

So a claim like "our sellers achieve higher prices than average" needs real evidence behind it. If you can't support a comparative or numerical claim, don't make it.

#### United Kingdom

The CAP Code's section on [misleading advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/type/non_broadcast/code_section/03.html) says marketing communications must not materially mislead. Marketers must hold documentary evidence to prove claims consumers are likely to regard as objective before publishing. The section also covers qualifications: marketing must not mislead by omitting significant limitations and qualifications, and qualifications must be presented clearly. That's directly relevant to calculator results and "free valuation" offers.

The same section has rules on the word "free": it must not be used if the consumer has to pay anything other than the unavoidable cost of responding. If your "free valuation" is only free when the owner lists with you, or carries other conditions, make that clear or don't call it free.

Both regulators' guidance depends on the facts, so check the current rules and take legal advice if you're unsure. This isn't legal advice.

### A before and after example

Here's an invented example of a valuation page headline and offer.

**Before:** "FREE instant business valuation! Find out what your business is REALLY worth in 60 seconds. We get our clients top dollar."

**After:** "What's your business worth? Get a confidential, indicative range from an experienced broker. Share a few figures and we'll call you within two working days to talk through how buyers would see your business. There's no charge for this conversation and no obligation to list. A formal written valuation is available as a separate service."

The second version sets accurate expectations, avoids unsupported claims and gives the owner a reason to talk to a person.

### Where the valuation page fits on your site

- **Link to it from your homepage** in the seller section, not just the footer.
- **Mention it on sector pages**: "Thinking about selling your HVAC business? Find out what it might be worth."
- **Send inquiries to the right broker automatically**, tagged by sector and timeline. My guide to [automating lead triage](/blog/automate-lead-triage-crm-workflows-make-zapier.html) explains how.
- **Follow up with useful content** for owners who aren't ready, such as how to prepare a business for sale.

For the rest of the seller journey, see my guide to [business broker websites that win seller listings](/blog/business-broker-website.html).

### How I can help

I build WordPress websites for business brokers and acquisition firms in the US and the UK, including valuation request pages, carefully labeled calculators, confidential inquiry forms and routing to the right broker. You can see more about my [websites for business brokers](/industries/business-brokers/) or browse [100+ sites in my portfolio](/work.html).

If you'd like a valuation page that brings in seller conversations, [get in touch](/#contact).
